criterion_notes.c1: Although the article is primarily a broad historical-political essay on South African civil society and 'people power' from the mid-1980s to 2011 across housing, labour, healthcare, electricity, and water, specific subsections (PDF Pages 12, 14-15, and 19-20) discuss household water service access, prepaid water meters, tariff affordability, and water disconnections in urban townships.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the essay broadly discusses governance, institutional, and municipal policy factors (apartheid local administration, post-1994 neoliberal commercialisation, cost-recovery campaigns, prepaid meters, and rising-block water tariffs) as drivers of township protest, which touches on governance topically, though plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper contains no empirical evidence (E05). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although brief narrative passages (PDF Pages 14-15 and 19) mention rule-type tariff and enforcement instruments (prepaid water meters, the 6,000-litre Free Basic Services allowance, convex rising-block water tariffs, and non-payment disconnections), the paper does not examine how these rules govern service access; instead, its analytical subject is macro-political ideology ('neoliberalism') and broad social movement mobilisation ('people power'), treating municipal service policies as unanalysed background and secondary protest grievances.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence (E05). The article is a historical-political narrative essay and commentary tracing South African civic and social movements from the 1980s to 2011. It presents no primary data collection, no empirical research methodology, and no systematic empirical synthesis, relying instead on secondary literature, party/government documents, and newspaper articles (e.g., Washington Post, New York Times, The Economist).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report original or systematically synthesised empirical study outcomes on water or sanitation access; it only cites secondary summary statistics in passing (such as water disconnection estimates and Durban household consumption drops from Bond & Dugard 2008 and a 2003 New York Times article) to illustrate grievances motivating social protests.
criterion_notes.c5: As a non-empirical political-historical commentary essay, there is no identifiable empirical study design, no defined sample or analytical unit of analysis, and no structured exposure-outcome evaluation.

rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Bond (2012) is a macro-historical and political narrative essay tracing South African 'people power', anti-apartheid civic associations, and post-apartheid social movements from the mid-1980s to 2011. While brief passages cite newspaper reports and secondary studies (e.g., New York Times 2003; Bond & Dugard 2008) regarding Orange Farm prepaid water meters, convex rising-block water tariffs, disconnections, and Durban water consumption to illustrate triggers of township protests, the paper contains no primary empirical data, no identifiable empirical research methodology, and no systematic empirical synthesis. It also treats municipal policy largely as macro-political background to social movement mobilisation rather than examining a rule-type water access mechanism, so it is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording.
